<reflection>
After two experiments varying catalyst concentration (0.01 M and 0.1 M) with substrate at 1.0 M and no initial product, the fitting results show that many mechanisms still have very similar negative log-likelihoods, with M7 currently the best but closely followed by several deactivation mechanisms (M20, M11, M14, M9, etc.). The differences are small, indicating that the data so far does not strongly discriminate among the top 15+ mechanisms. The aim of the second experiment (increased catalyst) did shift the rankings slightly but not enough to rule out many candidates. Therefore, a new experimental dimension is needed to break the degeneracy. Adding initial product will probe reversibility and product-dependent deactivation, which are features that differentiate many of the remaining mechanisms. By keeping substrate and catalyst the same as in the first experiment, we can isolate the effect of product and directly compare with the product-free case.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
Introducing a high initial product concentration (0.5 M) while keeping substrate at 1.0 M and catalyst at 0.01 M will test several key aspects: (1) Reverse reaction rates: mechanisms with reversible catalytic steps (all except deactivation steps) will show a slower net forward rate, and the extent of slowing depends on the equilibrium constant. (2) Product inhibition/deactivation: mechanisms with explicit product deactivation (M12, M17) or product-dependent steps may exhibit altered kinetics, such as faster decay of activity. (3) For mechanisms without product sensitivity (e.g., M7, which has no direct product binding except possibly through reverse steps), the effect may be different. Comparing this run with run 1 (same conditions but P=0) will reveal the influence of product on the time course. This condition avoids extreme substrate or catalyst concentrations and targets a new dimension (product concentration) that has not been explored, making it informative across many mechanisms simultaneously.
</hypothesis>
